title: How Mummies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how mummies work, covering post-death decomposition (autolysis, putrefaction), natural preservation by ice, sand, and cold dry conditions, and the development of Egyptian mummification from accidental desiccation in sand to caskets, evisceration, natron dehydration, oil-injection budget mummification, bandaging, cartonage and funerary masks, and burial rites. They also survey other mummies: Chinchorro people of Chile, Incas' child sacrifices (the Maiden), Guanajuato-style Mexican mummy museum, Lady Dai-style Chinese mummies, Lenin's embalming, Catholic incorruptibles, and plastination (Body Worlds). The episode closes with King Tut's tomb curse myths, Dr. Bob Brier's replication experiment, and listener mail from Maddie about her friend Casey.

segments.title: Opening banter and mummies follow-up
segments.summary: The hosts open the show, recall the earlier fossils episode where desiccated remains were mentioned, and say mummies are a natural follow-up topic.

segments.title: Post-death decomposition and natural preservation
segments.summary: Autolysis and putrefaction are described as stages of decay after death. Warm humid climates speed decomposition while cold dry conditions slow it. Examples of natural mummies include the Ice Man, Tollund Man, and sand preservation.

segments.title: Origins of Egyptian mummification
segments.summary: Early Egyptians buried bodies in hot sand, which preserved them accidentally. Belief that preservation meant a preserved spirit led to deliberate burial in sand, then to caskets, which caused the bodies to rot. This prompted the development of artificial embalming techniques.

segments.title: Step-by-step elite Egyptian mummification process
segments.summary: The body is washed in the Nile at the Ibu, then taken to the per-nefer (house of mummification) where the brain is removed through the nose with hooks and the organs are removed through an incision on the left side. Organs are preserved and placed in canopic jars, except the heart. The body is stuffed with incense, straw, and other materials.

segments.title: Natron dehydration, bandaging, and burial rites
segments.summary: The body is covered in natron for about forty days to dry it out. It is then stuffed, sewn, coated with resin, and bandaged in linen over one or two weeks, with amulets placed among the wrappings. A cartonage and funerary mask are added, and the mummy undergoes a funeral with the ceremony of the mouth before burial in a tomb, often with a curse inscribed.

segments.title: Budget mummification
segments.summary: Poorer Egyptians received a cheaper process where oil was injected into the body cavities, the orifices were plugged, and the oil drained out with liquefied tissue after a few days.

segments.title: King Tut curse and mold theory
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1920s excitement over King Tut's tomb opened by Howard Carter, the supposed curse, and a German microbiologist's theory that mold spores could cause illness. They mention deaths of people involved and unwrapping parties.

segments.title: Other ancient mummies worldwide
segments.summary: The Chinchorro people of northern Chile made mummies roughly two thousand years before the Egyptians, using dismemberment and black mud coating. The Incas sacrificed children, including the mummy known as the Maiden. Chinese mummies include Lady Dai and Indo-Iranian people found in the Tarim region. A Mexican mummy museum is noted.

segments.title: Modern mummies, plastination, and incorruptibles
segments.summary: Lenin's embalmed body in the Kremlin and Evita Perón's wax-replaced body are discussed. Catholic incorruptible corpses are mentioned. Plastination, which replaces water and lipids with polymers, is used for exhibits like Body Worlds in Atlanta.

segments.title: Bob Brier's chicken mummification experiment
segments.summary: Egyptologist Bob Brier replicated the Egyptian technique on a chicken at the University of Maryland School of Medicine and learned that the shriveled look comes from the mummification process itself rather than from long burial.

segments.title: Further resources and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the HowStuffWorks mummies article, WikiHow, and Cool Stuff on the Planet's mummy museum coverage, then sign off.

segments.title: Listener mail from Maddie
segments.summary: Twelve-year-old Maddie writes in asking for a shout-out to her friend Casey, who has a leg tumor, and his pet rooster Lewis. She also suggests a story about a French queen. The hosts respond and invite mummy stories by email.
